k-accomplished.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> climbs a <radical>road</radical>, its surface <radical>split</radical> into ruts of packed <radical>earth</radical>. The flock keeps stalling, but the last one clears the rise: the job is <kanji>accomplished</kanji>.
k-accomplished.reading_mnemonic: Tatsu is the drover who marks the top of every hill the same way: one slap on the gatepost and a barked 「<reading>たつ</reading>」 — done, next. He has said it at every gate between here and the coast. たつ means it is finished.

k-ancestor.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>altar</radical> stands on the left. Beside it, an <radical>eye</radical> lies flat above a line of <radical>ground</radical> — a portrait propped over the offerings. Somebody long dead looks back at you off that shelf: your <kanji>ancestor</kanji>.
k-ancestor.reading_mnemonic: So is the small catch of sound the incense makes when it takes light at the altar — 「<reading>そ</reading>」 — and for a second the eye in the portrait seems to move. One syllable, once a year, for the ancestor. そ.

k-breath.meaning_mnemonic: You jab a finger at your own <radical>self</radical> to answer for something. Your <radical>heart</radical> pounds beneath it, working overtime from the shock. What rushes between the two, in and out, is your <kanji>breath</kanji>.
k-breath.reading_mnemonic: Soku is the swimmer who comes up after far too long under and takes one enormous ragged gulp — 「<reading>そく</reading>」 — nose first, heart going like a hammer. That is what a breath you badly needed sounds like. そく.

k-daughter.meaning_mnemonic: A young <radical>woman</radical> reaches the door, ready to leave. A strict house rule ends up <radical>stopping</radical> her before nine. She sighs and stays inside, still somebody's <kanji>daughter</kanji>.
k-daughter.reading_mnemonic: Jou is how the neighbours refer to her, drawn out and a shade too formal — 「<reading>じょう</reading>」. It is the address for a girl of good family who is not allowed out tonight. She hears じょう and rolls her eyes.

k-daytime.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Daytime</kanji> is just the distance a <radical>ruler</radical> measures upward from the <radical>daybreak</radical> line to wherever the sun has climbed by now.
k-daytime.reading_mnemonic: Chuu, the loyal mouse with the tiny topknot, guards the sundial for the whole bright stretch of the day. When the shadow shrinks to nothing, he marks the middle of it with one proud <reading>ちゅう</reading>. That squeak is really just him biting a rice cracker, a single loud <reading>chew</reading>.

k-doctor.meaning_mnemonic: Whoever pulls the <radical>arrow</radical> out of you and shuts it inside a <radical>hiding enclosure</radical> has done a <kanji>doctor</kanji>'s entire job.
k-doctor.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail a hiker catches a stray arrow graze, and the doctor in the group digs a first-aid kit out of her pack. The moment the antiseptic touches the cut the hiker yelps a sharp <reading>eek</reading>, and it echoes off the rocks as <reading>い</reading>.

k-end.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the <radical>tree</radical>: a <radical>stick</radical> straight up, branches <radical>split</radical> aside. A <radical>lid</radical> stroke lies atop, longer than the <radical>one</radical> below — the twig's last inch: the <kanji>end</kanji>.
k-end.reading_mnemonic: Matsu is the woodsman who only ever takes the tip. He climbs the whole tree, snips the last bud off the top of it, and calls down 「<reading>まつ</reading>」 to say he has got there. まつ means there is nothing above him.

k-evening.meaning_mnemonic: A curved hill holds a setting moon, sliced by one falling line. The light fades to blue as hush settles into <radical>evening</radical>. This whole little picture simply means <kanji>evening</kanji>.
k-evening.reading_mnemonic: Seki comes out onto his step at this hour every night, and you hear him before you see him — that wet, rattling 「<reading>せき</reading>」 of a cough carrying right down the street. When せき starts up, the light has gone.

k-father.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>father</radical> radical and the <kanji>father</kanji> kanji are the exact same shape and the same word, so this one comes free.
k-father.reading_mnemonic: Your father stands over the barbecue for a whole hot hour, and when the last plate is full he drops into a chair with a long <reading>ふ</reading> of relief. It is the exact sound a worn-out dad makes, a slow <reading>phew</reading> pushed out through the smoke. The kids know that breath means dinner is finally served.

k-friend.meaning_mnemonic: One stroke <radical>slides</radical> down from the top left across a bar of <radical>ground</radical>, met by a <radical>right hand</radical> rising underneath. Two hands close on each other, nobody paid, nobody in charge: that is a <kanji>friend</kanji>.
k-friend.reading_mnemonic: Yuu is always there before you, hand already out. He draws the greeting into a long two-beat call across the car park — 「<reading>ゆう</reading>」 — before you have shut the car door. ゆう means somebody is glad to see you.

k-gone.meaning_mnemonic: A mound of <radical>earth</radical> sits on top, underneath a sealed <radical>cocoon</radical> tucked out of sight. Whatever was inside wrapped up and went under the soil. Dig the mound over: nothing is left. It is <kanji>gone</kanji>.
k-gone.reading_mnemonic: Kyo is the magician who buries things and cannot get them back. He taps the mound, says 「<reading>きょ</reading>」 with a flourish, and that is genuinely the end of the trick. No reappearance, no second half. きょ, and it is gone.

k-he.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>step</radical> at the left edge, beside a hide hauled off in one sheet — all <radical>skin</radical>, no animal left. Someone walked past carrying it and is already down the road. That man you point at and cannot name: <kanji>he</kanji>.
k-he.reading_mnemonic: Hii is the little intake of breath you make when the man in the skin cloak goes past without a word — 「<reading>ひ</reading>」. By the time you finish it, he is round the corner. Every time you catch sight of him: ひ.

k-heart.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>wide box</radical> of a room, shoved to the back with <radical>rice</radical> and something <radical>big</radical> on top. You walk through every room to reach it; nobody outside the family does. The deepest room is the <kanji>heart</kanji>.
k-heart.reading_mnemonic: Ou is the grandmother who lives in that back room and has not come out in years. Knock and you get one long syllable through the paper door — 「<reading>おう</reading>」 — meaning she heard you and no, you may not come in. おう, from the very back of the house.

k-husband.meaning_mnemonic: Take the <radical>big</radical> figure — the <radical>person</radical> with arms flung wide. Lay one bar on top like a <radical>lid</radical>, so <radical>two</radical> strokes sit there, not one: his topknot pin. Grown and married: <kanji>husband</kanji>.
k-husband.reading_mnemonic: Fu is the same breath out through the nose you learned from his father, inherited exactly — arms folded in the doorway, one 「<reading>ふ</reading>」, no further comment offered. Getting married did not change it in the slightest.

k-me.meaning_mnemonic: Deep in a <radical>thicket</radical> where every other <radical>person</radical> is hidden, the only one I can still point to is <kanji>me</kanji>.
k-me.reading_mnemonic: Lost in that same thicket, a hiker finally crashes out into the open, hugging one soggy paperback <reading>book</reading> to his chest. When the ranger asks whose it is, all he can gasp between breaths is <reading>ぼく</reading> — mine, that one is me.
k-me.description: As a first-person word this is used mainly by boys and men and stays casual, so it is out of place in formal writing or when you must be very polite. It grew out of an older, humble word for a servant.

k-mister.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>official</radical> whose <radical>mouth</radical> is always hanging open to bark one more order is exactly the man everyone is forced to call <kanji>mister</kanji>.
k-mister.reading_mnemonic: That same barking official trudges up the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine. The cats swarm him and web him into a fat silk <reading>cocoon</reading> in seconds, and every command he keeps shouting from inside now comes out as a muffled <reading>くん</reading>.
k-mister.description: Not a polite title. As a name-suffix it marks a junior, a classmate, or a young man rather than a superior. As a stand-alone word it is a familiar 'you' that can sound blunt with someone you barely know.

k-morning.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Morning</kanji> is the one stretch of the day when the striped light of <radical>sunrise</radical> is already up while the <radical>moon</radical> still hangs in the window.
k-morning.reading_mnemonic: Cho, the rooster who always oversleeps, finally crows <reading>ちょう</reading> from the fence rail just as the last of the moonlight fades. Every house on the mountain trail wakes to that one lazy <reading>Cho</reading>. It is the sound that tells you the day has already started.
k-morning.description: Beyond the daily sense, 朝 also names a dynasty or imperial court, and it turns up in words for a ruling era or reigning house. At this level only morning is tested.

k-mother.meaning_mnemonic: You already know the <radical>mother</radical> radical, so this <kanji>mother</kanji> kanji is a gift, the same seated figure with both children held tight.
k-mother.reading_mnemonic: A mother <reading>boa</reading> has coiled around her eggs on the mossy shrine steps, guarding them with no patience at all. Each time a shrine cat pads too close she lifts her head and gives one low, flat note, <reading>ぼ</reading>. The cats have learned that a mother's warning means back off.

k-night.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>lid</radical> is pulled across the sky, and a <radical>person</radical> slips under as the last <radical>evening</radical> drains away. Once the lid is on, nothing more gets in: no sun, no colour. The lid down over the evening: <kanji>night</kanji>.
k-night.reading_mnemonic: Ya is the yakitori man who only opens once the lid is down. The cart comes out of nowhere, the lantern goes up, and he calls one syllable into the dark — 「<reading>や</reading>」 — which is the entire advertisement. If you can hear や, it is night.

k-nightfall.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> on the left has been let off: the shape on the right squeezes from under the heavy lid, walking off <radical>exempt</radical>. Its shift is done; it drops below the roofline unbid. The sun excused from duty: <kanji>nightfall</kanji>.
k-nightfall.reading_mnemonic: Ban is the night watchman who takes over the moment the sun clocks off. He drags the gate shut and announces himself to the empty street — 「<reading>ばん</reading>」 — one flat syllable, every night, so you know the day is closed.

k-on-foot.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>step</radical> turns into a wild <radical>run</radical> down the road. There is no horse or cart anywhere in sight. So the whole trip happens <kanji>on foot</kanji>.
k-on-foot.reading_mnemonic: Toto the door-to-door turtle has never once taken a ride. He carries the sample doors on his shell and walks the entire round, and he announces himself at every house with the same syllable before he knocks — 「<reading>と</reading>」. と, and another mile.

k-private.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> leans on the left, tucked behind it a little <radical>cocoon</radical>, sealed tight. Nobody else knows it is there. You grew the crop in the open, then kept one seed back for yourself: <kanji>private</kanji>.
k-private.reading_mnemonic: Shi is the quiet one who keeps her own small field behind the house, and when anyone asks what she is growing in it she says 「<reading>し</reading>」 and closes the gate. Not rude, exactly. Whatever is in there is hers, and し is the only answer you are ever going to get.

k-second-1.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> stands in the field, thin at the very top. Someone plucks the <radical>small</radical> piece from its tip. That tiny sliver of time becomes one <kanji>second</kanji>.
k-second-1.reading_mnemonic: Byou is the hospital timekeeper with the stopwatch, and she counts out loud in a flat clipped bark — 「<reading>びょう</reading>」, びょう, びょう — one for every tick. She will not speed up and she will not stop. びょう is a single second landing.

k-submit.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> on the left; on the right <radical>two</radical> bars over <radical>ground</radical>, each on a <radical>stick</radical>, <radical>split</radical> into legs at the foot. A tray, lifted with both hands for somebody above to take: to <kanji>submit</kanji> a thing.
k-submit.reading_mnemonic: Kyou is the offering-bearer who never lowers the tray. He walks the entire length of the hall with it over his head, announcing himself at every pillar — 「<reading>きょう</reading>」 — until somebody finally takes the weight off him.

k-uncle.meaning_mnemonic: A stick of <radical>divination</radical> in the corner, a <radical>small</radical> mark beside it, a <radical>right hand</radical> scooping both up. He is the younger brother: not head of the family, so he gets the small share. Your <kanji>uncle</kanji>.
k-uncle.reading_mnemonic: Shuku is that uncle, and he arrives every year with the same trick. He shuffles the sticks, throws them down, sucks his teeth, and pronounces 「<reading>しゅく</reading>」 as though it settles the matter. Nobody knows what しゅく means. He will not explain.

k-what.meaning_mnemonic: Faced with a <radical>person</radical> who swears they <radical>can</radical> do absolutely anything, the only question left to ask is <kanji>what</kanji>.
k-what.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line outside Koichi's konbini and brags he can fix any broken machine. You point at the smoking till and ask <reading>か</reading>, meaning which part is even fixable. He just puffs a little flame and gives his only reply, a flat <reading>caw</reading>.

k-who.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Words</radical> stand on the left, on the right an <radical>old bird</radical> with its head cocked, waiting. You have talked for ten minutes and the bird still cannot tell which person you mean. It asks the only question left: <kanji>who</kanji>?
k-who.reading_mnemonic: Sui is the owl who works the gate. She leans down, blinks once, and hoots 「<reading>すい</reading>」, which in owl means name, please. Nobody gets past her without answering it. すい, すい, until you say who you are.

k-wife.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> sweeps her yard with a <radical>broom</radical> tied to a <radical>stick</radical>. She works until the bare <radical>ground</radical> is spotless. The neighbors call her the tidy <kanji>wife</kanji> of the house.
k-wife.reading_mnemonic: Sai is the one who actually decides. Ask her husband anything and he glances sideways at her first; she gives one flat 「<reading>さい</reading>」 and that is the answer on behalf of both of them. さい settles it.

k-yesterday.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> on the left, a <radical>stick</radical> upright on the right with one <radical>slide</radical> of a stroke off it. That stick is a sundial, its shadow scratched beside. The sun moved on; the mark left behind is <kanji>yesterday</kanji>.
k-yesterday.reading_mnemonic: Saku is the old gardener who checks his shadow-stick every dawn and then grumbles about how much better the light was 「<reading>さく</reading>」 — his one-word shorthand for the day before. Nothing is ever as good as さく was.

k-zero.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> kneels on the wet <radical>ground</radical> as <radical>rain</radical> pours down. A clerk presses his <radical>stamp</radical> on the puddle, and the ink washes away. Nothing is left to count, so he writes <kanji>zero</kanji>.
k-zero.reading_mnemonic: Rei is that clerk. She is scrupulously polite about it — a small bow, a murmured 「<reading>れい</reading>」 — and then she inks the nothing into your row and moves down the line. れい, bow, zero. She has done it forty times today.

k-employee.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>employee</kanji> is just one more <radical>mouth</radical> the company has to feed with its own <radical>money</radical>.
k-employee.reading_mnemonic: The gatekeeper is a retired innkeeper everyone calls <reading>Inn</reading>. She grunts <reading>いん</reading> every time she stamps a badge — one grunt per hire. By dusk, her voice is gone from saying it all day.
k-employee.description: 員 rarely stands alone as a word for 'employee' — it is a suffix meaning roughly 'a person belonging to,' always riding on a job title, company, or club, closer to '-er' than to a stand-alone noun.

k-tooth.meaning_mnemonic: Grains of <radical>rice</radical> that <radical>stop</radical> inside the <radical>open box</radical> of your jaw were caught there by one <kanji>tooth</kanji>.
k-tooth.reading_mnemonic: One shrine cat, nicknamed <reading>Shii</reading> for the hiss she makes mid-gnaw, clamps onto the bell rim and hisses <reading>し</reading> through the gap where a tooth used to be.

k-body.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> is really just a <radical>book</radical> of bones and organs bound into a single <kanji>body</kanji>.
k-body.reading_mnemonic: Someone always loops a spare <reading>tie</reading> around the training dummy's neck before drills, and the coach barks <reading>たい</reading> to snap the team to attention — same dummy, same crooked tie, every single practice.

k-thing.meaning_mnemonic: Anything that is a <radical>cow</radical> and <radical>not</radical> a person gets filed away as a mere <kanji>thing</kanji>.
k-thing.reading_mnemonic: Koichi holds up a single lost <reading>boot</reading> from the bin and grunts <reading>ぶつ</reading> — the general word for 'thing,' because after six unclaimed months, calling it a boot feels oddly specific.

k-meal.meaning_mnemonic: A plate of <radical>food</radical> is the <radical>opposite</radical> of an empty one, and closing that gap is what a <kanji>meal</kanji> is for.
k-meal.reading_mnemonic: Han, the half-and-half chef, slices your whole dinner clean down the center before you can protest — that's just how he works here. You call out his name, <reading>Han</reading>, and he answers with a proud <reading>はん</reading>, holding up two identical plates like it settles the matter.

k-tea.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a steaming cup: delicate <radical>grass</radical> leaves curling up top like visible steam, a little <radical>person</radical> warming his hands round a <radical>tree</radical>-carved cup below. That curling steam over the cup is the whole picture: <kanji>tea</kanji>.
k-tea.reading_mnemonic: A dance instructor spins through the tearoom mid cha-cha lesson, a full teacup balanced on his palm. He counts the beat out loud — 「<reading>ちゃ</reading>」-cha-cha — until the cup tips and the lesson ends the same soaked way every time.

k-hit.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a dart thrown with quiet <radical>esteem</radical> for its own aim, flight feathers up top, and a <radical>broom</radical>-shaped tail sweeping it dead center into the target below. One clean throw, no wobble: a direct <kanji>hit</kanji>.
k-hit.reading_mnemonic: The dart thrower celebrates his bullseye by kicking the target stand in triumph and instantly regrets it, hopping and hissing through his teeth: <reading>とう</reading>, my <reading>toe</reading>, my <reading>toe</reading>! Somehow he still lands the next throw dead center.

k-ill.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sickness</radical> bad enough to put you in a <radical>third class</radical> bed is what it looks like to be genuinely <kanji>ill</kanji>.
k-ill.reading_mnemonic: The former beauty-pageant queen lies flat under the sickroom's too-short blanket, moaning into her pillow. This is the least glamorous she has ever looked: 「<reading>びょう</reading>」, she groans, sounding exactly like the first half of <reading>beauty</reading> gone hoarse.

k-section.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 部 as a squat filing cabinet: a <radical>stand</radical> strut over a slot like an open <radical>mouth</radical>, beside a little <radical>village</radical> of drawers. A clerk yanks the wrong drawer, gets buried in someone else's forms, and slams shut the one marked for his own <kanji>section</kanji>.
k-section.reading_mnemonic: A moth called <reading>Bu</reading> gets shut inside that same drawer overnight and beats its wings against the forms, the frantic drumming going <reading>ぶ</reading>, <reading>ぶ</reading>, <reading>ぶ</reading>, until dawn finally opens the drawer and lets it stagger free.

k-pedestal.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 台 as a squat stone pedestal: a <radical>cocoon</radical>-shaped knob on top, over a wide <radical>mouth</radical> of a base bolted to the ground. Workers winch a bronze statue onto it, and the block doesn't budge under the weight: solid, built for holding something up — a <kanji>pedestal</kanji>.
k-pedestal.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Dai</reading>, the giant baby, climbs onto that same pedestal to pose like a statue. One stomp cracks the stone with a boom that rattles windows, and he wails <reading>だい</reading>, <reading>だい</reading> as the block crumbles beneath him.

k-courtyard.meaning_mnemonic: The open ground between the <radical>shelter</radical> and the <radical>courts</radical> is the <kanji>courtyard</kanji> everybody has to cross.
k-courtyard.reading_mnemonic: The groundskeeper, named <reading>Tei</reading>, sprints after the goat squatting in the courtyard, tripping over the raked gravel and yelling <reading>てい</reading>, <reading>てい</reading> with every failed lunge, gravel spraying across the whole swept quiet.

k-turn.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 番 as a ticket dispenser bolted to a wall, its slots ruled like a tiny <radical>rice field</radical>, spitting out numbered slips kept strictly <radical>separate</radical>. Customers file into line by number, nobody out of place: the pure order of your <kanji>turn</kanji>.
k-turn.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a guard named <reading>Ban</reading> slams a wooden stamp onto the counter each time a new number is called. The crack echoes <reading>ばん</reading> through the shop as the line shuffles forward, one turn at a time.

k-empty.meaning_mnemonic: When the entire <radical>construction</radical> job is digging one <radical>hole</radical>, the thing you have built is an <kanji>empty</kanji> space.
k-empty.reading_mnemonic: Still stuck at the summit, the hiker slumps against the machine and lets out a long, pigeon-like <reading>coo</reading> up at the empty sky. 「<reading>くう</reading>」, rising and hollow, over and over, until it's the only sound left on the mountain.

k-brush-stroke.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>brush-stroke</kanji> is <radical>one</radical> line with a <radical>reason</radical>, laid down inside the <radical>open box</radical> of the page.
k-brush-stroke.reading_mnemonic: Back in the art room, the teacher looks at the smeared frame and can only manage a flat, deflated <reading>gah</reading> — <reading>が</reading> — the sound of someone giving up on a critique before it starts. He staples a ribbon to it anyway and calls it finished.

k-reflect.meaning_mnemonic: When the <radical>sun</radical> sits at the exact <radical>center</radical> of the sky, the water below throws back its clearest <kanji>reflect</kanji>ion.
k-reflect.reading_mnemonic: Startled by his own doubled face in the water, the fisherman yelps 「<reading>Ay</reading>」 — 「<reading>えい</reading>」. The river throws the sound straight back at him a beat later, flat and unbothered, same as it did with the light.

k-roof.meaning_mnemonic: Wherever your <radical>body</radical> finally <radical>arrive</radical>s at the end of the day, the thing over it is a <kanji>roof</kanji>.
k-roof.reading_mnemonic: Weeks later, the tarp is still up, now painted with a crude little <reading>oak</reading> tree Koichi drew himself — <reading>おく</reading> — because customers kept asking what was holding the whole roof together. Nobody has the heart to tell him it's just tarp and string.

k-inst.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>perfect</radical> row of buildings up on the <radical>hill</radical> is how every <kanji>Inst</kanji>itute wants to be seen.
k-inst.reading_mnemonic: At the same window, the visor cat's ink stamp has half-dried, so every ticket comes out a pale <reading>いん</reading>. She grumbles it sounds like <reading>bean</reading> paste smeared thin, and refuses to fetch a new pad before the shrine's afternoon bell.

k-bureau.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>body</radical> that answers every <radical>phrase</radical> you say with another form to fill in is working in a <kanji>bureau</kanji>.
k-bureau.reading_mnemonic: Wedged into that same booth, a customer three forms deep chokes on chalky bureau dust drifting off the tax stacks, coughing out something between a wheeze and <reading>きょく</reading>. Koichi just nods, because everyone who reaches window three sounds exactly like they're trying to say <reading>choke</reading>.

k-convenience.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> who can <radical>renew</radical> anything for you without leaving the counter is selling pure <kanji>convenience</kanji>.
k-convenience.reading_mnemonic: The badger's slam sends the vending machine's change chute rattling out coins. The hiker who planned to buy one — a guy named <reading>Ben</reading> — just mutters 「<reading>べん</reading>」 under his breath, resigned to waiting outside in the rain.

k-building.meaning_mnemonic: Put a kitchen of <radical>food</radical> under the same roof as a <radical>bureaucrat</radical> and you need a <kanji>building</kanji> big enough for both.
k-building.reading_mnemonic: The gym teacher, thrilled with his new marble domain, now calls himself 「<reading>かん</reading>」 instead of coach — loosely, <reading>Khan</reading>. He blows his whistle from the staircase every morning like a monarch addressing the badminton court below.

k-near.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 近 as a signpost arrow, chopped short by an <radical>axe</radical>, that curled back along the <radical>road</radical> to jab at your own boots. On the mountain trail, the vending machine you swore was another hour up turns out one switchback away: <kanji>near</kanji>.
k-near.reading_mnemonic: At that vending machine, the hiker's little brother — pure <reading>kin</reading>, tagging along everywhere — presses his face to the glass and chants the machine's name like a drumbeat: <reading>きん</reading>. He is always, always this close.

k-slow.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> dragging its whole <radical>body</radical> up the <radical>road</radical> makes every journey behind it <kanji>slow</kanji>.
k-slow.reading_mnemonic: The class hamster, <reading>Chi</reading>, is let loose to race him and loses on purpose, wheezing one flat unimpressed <reading>ち</reading> at the finish line — same track, same dragging in dead last.

k-seethe.meaning_mnemonic: Charge a <radical>dollar</radical> for one cup of <radical>water</radical> and watch the whole queue <kanji>seethe</kanji>.

k-traffic.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>walled path</radical> feeding onto one open <radical>road</radical> is where all of the <kanji>traffic</kanji> ends up.

k-severance.reading_mnemonic: A fisherman named <reading>Dan</reading> stands at the riverbank when his line goes slack. He shouts <reading>だん</reading> — the exact sound of a taut line snapping in half, sharp and final.

k-stubborn.meaning_mnemonic: Anybody who argues from the <radical>beginning</radical> using nothing but their own <radical>head</radical> is being <kanji>stubborn</kanji>.

k-accustomed.meaning_mnemonic: Let the same thing <radical>pierce</radical> your <radical>heart</radical> often enough and you will get <kanji>accustomed</kanji> to it.

k-overdo.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>crooked mouth</radical> retelling the story the whole length of the <radical>road</radical> is certain to <kanji>overdo</kanji> it.

k-period.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>That</radical> same <radical>moon</radical> coming round to where it started marks the end of one <kanji>period</kanji>.

She only laughs on the ring, never between, so her giggle marks that same fixed moment each time.

k-scold.meaning_mnemonic: One <radical>mouth</radical> going at you for the <radical>seven</radical>th time has stopped being advice and become a <kanji>scold</kanji>ing.

k-praise.meaning_mnemonic: Wrapping somebody in fine <radical>clothing</radical> to <radical>protect</radical> them from criticism is one way to <kanji>praise</kanji> them.
k-praise.reading_mnemonic: The shrine's caretaker, nicknamed <reading>Whoa</reading> because it's the only thing she ever says, watches the bell hum with approval. She breathes out a satisfied <reading>ほう</reading>, her robe still settling.

k-apologize.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Words</radical> you <radical>shoot</radical> off before thinking are exactly the ones you have to <kanji>apologize</kanji> for later.

k-apologize.description: This kanji covers more than sorry: the same character also carries formal thanks and, in some compounds, an outright refusal or decline. Underneath all three is one idea, a formal spoken response rather than plain regret, so context decides whether it reads as apology, gratitude, or a firm no.

k-counter-for.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>bow</radical> strung for a <radical>long</radical> shot is the sort of thing you need a <kanji>counter for bows</kanji> to tally.

k-counter-for.description: As a counter, this kanji counts things held taut by a string, such as bows and stringed instruments, not flat sheets or long thin objects, which take other counters. The verb sense stretch or spread is the same idea: pulling something tight, which is why the same character became the counting word for anything strung that way.

k-wait.meaning_mnemonic: Every <radical>step</radical> up to the <radical>Buddhist temple</radical> already has somebody standing on it, so you <kanji>wait</kanji>.

k-harmony.meaning_mnemonic: Enough <radical>grain</radical> for every <radical>mouth</radical> in the village buys a whole season of <kanji>harmony</kanji>.

k-harmony.description: 和 alone usually means harmony or peace, but as a prefix on other words it commonly means Japanese-style - Japanese food, a Japanese-style room - describing where something comes from rather than describing peacefulness itself.

k-pour.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Water</radical> for the <radical>lord</radical> is the one cup you never <kanji>pour</kanji> carelessly.

k-clothing.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>month</radical> of wear, a maker's <radical>stamp</radical> and a <radical>right hand</radical> mending it is the life of one piece of <kanji>clothing</kanji>.

k-clothing.description: 服 by itself almost always means clothing, as in everyday words for Western-style clothes or a uniform. The senses obey and admit only appear buried inside fixed multi-character compounds about submission or confession - standing alone, this character just means clothes.

k-bow.reading_mnemonic: A boy named <reading>Kyu</reading> lines up his shot on the sports field, and the string gives a sharp <reading>きゅう</reading> as it snaps back into place, leaving nothing but that one clean sound behind.

k-fur.meaning_mnemonic: A dog sheds a single strand of <radical>fur</radical> onto the porch. Wind lifts it and twists it into a tight curl. That stray curling strand is one piece of <kanji>fur</kanji>.
k-fur.reading_mnemonic: Back at the vending machine, a hiker named <reading>Moe</reading> picks the stray wisp off his sweaty arm for the third time this climb. He groans <reading>もう</reading>, long and tired, dragging the sound out like his own name stretched thin. Loose fur keeps finding him no matter how high he climbs.

k-fish.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>fish</kanji> is the only animal that will <radical>crouch</radical> in a flooded <radical>rice field</radical> until the water is gone and the <radical>fire</radical> is licking the bottom of the pan.
k-fish.reading_mnemonic: A rockhound crouched at the riverbank is splitting open a <reading>geode</reading> when a fat carp launches out of the shallows and slaps her flat across the face. She topples backward with a startled <reading>ぎょ</reading>, and the fish flops calmly back in as if nothing happened.

k-yellow.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi forgets an oil lantern burning behind the konbini shelf. All night its glass glows a soft <radical>yellow</radical>, brighter than the fluorescent lights above. By morning the whole shelf is stained <kanji>yellow</kanji>.
k-yellow.reading_mnemonic: Koichi restocks the shelf by lantern light, counting under his breath: <reading>こう</reading>. It comes out low and steady, exactly like a pigeon's <reading>coo</reading>, over and over until every row is full again.

k-dart.meaning_mnemonic: At the fair, a vendor yanks his <radical>arrow</radical> out of a ruined pumpkin. Its feathers still splay and the point is still sharp. He flings it at the fence instead and calls it a <kanji>dart</kanji>.
k-dart.reading_mnemonic: Back at the fair, Shea guards the fence where the runaway shaft first landed. Anyone who reaches for it too fast gets a sharp <reading>し</reading> — flat, quick, cutting the sentence off like a blade through pumpkin. It sounds exactly like her name, <reading>Shea</reading>, minus the vowel.

k-capital.meaning_mnemonic: A city planner caps her model tower with a stone <radical>lid</radical>. Under it she props open a stone <radical>mouth</radical> as the gate. The whole model is so <radical>small</radical> it fits in her palm, a tiny <kanji>capital</kanji>.
k-capital.reading_mnemonic: At the ceremony, a boy named <reading>Kyo</reading> knocks the whole miniature capital off the table. It shatters on the floor, and all he can do is groan <reading>きょう</reading>, one long syllable of dread, as the tiny lid and gate pieces roll under the desks.

k-park.meaning_mnemonic: A groundskeeper drapes a <radical>clothing</radical> sheet over the flowerbeds like a tent. He stakes it down with a wooden <radical>earth</radical> marker so it will not blow away. Rain pools in a stone <radical>mouth</radical> fountain, turning the plot into his <kanji>park</kanji>.
k-park.reading_mnemonic: Back at the new park, gardener <reading>Enji</reading> trips over the fountain's hose and face-plants into the flowerbed. Muffled through a mouthful of dirt, all that comes out is a long <reading>えん</reading>, and the shirt-roof tent collapses on top of him.

k-ship.meaning_mnemonic: A dockhand splits a log into <radical>eight</radical> pieces with one swing. He wedges them along the hull of a <radical>boat</radical> to patch a leak. Then he bolts on a hatch shaped like a <radical>mouth</radical>, finishing his little <kanji>ship</kanji>.
k-ship.reading_mnemonic: Down at the dock, the sailor <reading>Sen</reading> hears the hatch slam onto his thumb and hisses a long <reading>せん</reading> through his teeth, hopping on one foot as the boat rocks against the pier.

k-angle.meaning_mnemonic: A carpenter drags his <radical>angle</radical> gauge to every crooked joint on a birdhouse. Thirty degrees here, ninety there, no two joints match. He shrugs and calls every mismatched joint a perfect <kanji>angle</kanji>.
k-angle.reading_mnemonic: Back at the workshop, the carpenter's uncle, always in a <reading>khaki</reading> jacket, grabs the gauge to fix the leaning birdhouse himself. He measures one corner, grunts <reading>かく</reading>, and nails it anyway, angle be damned. It still leans, but now it leans in his signature khaki style.

k-picture.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> ducks into a silk shed as a <radical>cocoon</radical> splits open. She pulls out <radical>two</radical> threads and crosses them on a frame. The tangled <radical>thread</radical> slowly becomes a <kanji>picture</kanji>.
k-picture.reading_mnemonic: The embroiderer everyone calls <reading>Kai</reading> signs every finished piece with his initial stitched in the corner: a tiny looped <reading>かい</reading>. Collectors say you can spot his work from across the room, that little loop of thread is his signature every time.

k-meat.meaning_mnemonic: A hungry cat stares through the butcher's window at two hanging slabs of <radical>meat</radical>. It leaps and paws at the glass, but the hooks hold firm. All the cat ever sees swinging inside is <kanji>meat</kanji>.
k-meat.reading_mnemonic: The butcher, whose name tag just says <reading>Nick</reading>, finally chases the cat off with a broom, growling <reading>にく</reading> at it like a curse word. He rehangs the swinging slabs and locks the frame before the cat tries its luck again.

k-door.meaning_mnemonic: Toto the turtle sells a sample <radical>door</radical> that never stays shut. He chases it down every street as it swings open again and again. The whole town now knows him by that one runaway <kanji>door</kanji>.
k-door.reading_mnemonic: Outside that same konbini, Toto scrapes his shell along the loose sill trying to force a sale, and each scrape knocks out the same hollow sound: <reading>coh</reading>, <reading>こ</reading>. Shoppers wince every time but can't stop hearing it after they've left. Toto just shrugs it off as free advertising.

k-autumn.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> leans over and drops onto the <radical>fire</radical> burning beside the field. It catches fast and sends smoke drifting over the empty rows. That smoky smell means <kanji>autumn</kanji> has arrived.
k-autumn.reading_mnemonic: A scarecrow standing in the smoking field flaps its sleeves at circling crows and yells <reading>shoo</reading>, <reading>しゅう</reading>, over and over until they scatter. Smoke from the burning stalks stings its painted eyes, but it keeps shouting anyway — the last of the grain only survives if somebody protects it.

k-feathers.meaning_mnemonic: A startled duck yanks out a <radical>feather</radical> and it drifts onto the pond. The wind tugs more loose until dozens follow it down. Soon the whole pond is coated in floating <kanji>feathers</kanji>.
k-feathers.reading_mnemonic: The fisherman stares at his soggy catch and groans <reading>ooh</reading>, <reading>う</reading>, disgusted at wasting good bait on nothing but down. He flings the pair back toward the water, where the duck has already forgotten the whole ordeal and gone back to preening at the pond's edge.

k-bird.meaning_mnemonic: A clumsy <radical>bird</radical> waddles into the convenience store, wings tucked like it is cold. It flops onto the rice ball shelf with a thud. The clerk sighs and carries the <kanji>bird</kanji> back outside.
k-bird.reading_mnemonic: Everyone at the konbini calls the night clerk <reading>Chow</reading>. He barks <reading>ちょう</reading> at the bird every single night, like he's calling a stray in for dinner. It never once listens.

k-chirp.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>bird</radical> lands on the goalpost during recess. Its beak opens into a wide <radical>mouth</radical> like a square hole. Out comes a piercing <kanji>chirp</kanji> that stops the game.
k-chirp.reading_mnemonic: The gym teacher on duty is called <reading>May</reading>. She blows her whistle and shouts <reading>めい</reading> every time that shriek cuts through practice. Nobody on the field mentions that the bird started it.

k-ri.meaning_mnemonic: The furthest you can still make out a village by <radical>sun</radical>light is roughly one <kanji>ri</kanji>.
k-ri.reading_mnemonic: The village elder who waves hikers toward the paddies goes by <reading>Lee</reading>. Every exhausted hiker calls back a grateful <reading>り</reading> as thanks. That's as much of his name as anyone manages out of breath. He just nods toward the shade.

k-snow.meaning_mnemonic: The falling <radical>rain</radical> freezes solid before it lands outside the temple. A monk grabs a <radical>broom</radical> and sweeps the icy drops into soft white drifts. He won't ring the bell until every trace of <kanji>snow</kanji> is gone.
k-snow.reading_mnemonic: The groundskeeper everyone calls <reading>Set</reading> mutters <reading>せつ</reading> under his breath every time he has to shovel the steps again. By dawn the drifts are back, deeper than before, and so is his sigh.

k-number.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> drops a bag of <radical>rice</radical> and grains spill everywhere. Her <radical>trailing foot</radical> drags them into neat <radical>chevron</radical> stripes. She <radical>taps</radical> each stripe with her toe to find the final <kanji>number</kanji>.
k-number.reading_mnemonic: Back in that gym, the scorekeeper — a woman named <reading>Sue</reading> — squints at the tally and groans <reading>すう</reading>, dragging the sound out like she dreads the total. The same scattered rice still crunches under her shoes.

k-summer.meaning_mnemonic: Your bare feet scorch on the baked <radical>ground</radical>. You point at <radical>self</radical> and swear the heat does not bother you. Then your <radical>trailing foot</radical> drags behind, and the stubborn heat becomes <kanji>summer</kanji>.
k-summer.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, sags on a power line above that same baked ground. Too hot even for him, he cracks his beak and a weak puff of flame escapes with a scorched <reading>か</reading>. That tired flame-cough is how you remember summer's reading, <reading>か</reading>.

k-winter.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>drop</radical> hangs frozen off the fence, refusing to fall. The same cold locks your <radical>trailing foot</radical> in mid-step. Everything holds still in the grip of <kanji>winter</kanji>.
k-winter.reading_mnemonic: Back at that fence, a shivering dog named Toby paws at his own frozen <reading>toe</reading> and yelps <reading>とう</reading>, breath crystallizing mid-air just like the drop dangling above him.

k-cloud.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Rain</radical> falls onto the <radical>ground</radical> where <radical>two</radical> silkworms spin themselves into a <radical>cocoon</radical>. The cocoon soaks up water until it swells and floats free. It drifts upward and puffs into a <kanji>cloud</kanji>.
k-cloud.reading_mnemonic: That swollen cocoon keeps drifting away from the ground like a stray <reading>balloon</reading>, and everyone at the window mutters <reading>うん</reading> in surprise as it floats past, still dripping rain.

k-face.meaning_mnemonic: You <radical>stand</radical> at the edge of a <radical>cliff</radical> holding a pot <radical>lid</radical> full of paint. You dab <radical>three</radical> quick streaks onto a giant stone <radical>head</radical> beside you. Those streaks blink open into a grinning <kanji>face</kanji>.
k-face.reading_mnemonic: Back on the cliff edge, a photographer named <reading>Gan</reading> leans in too close for the shot and slips on loose gravel. He yelps a sharp <reading>がん</reading> as he grabs the rock ledge, dangling right below the sleepy head on the page.

k-springtime.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> steps onto the thawed <radical>ground</radical> after a long winter. They plant <radical>two</radical> sticks and throw their arms out as <radical>big</radical> as they can. The <radical>sun</radical> climbs higher each morning until mud season turns into <kanji>springtime</kanji>.
k-springtime.reading_mnemonic: A groundhog named <reading>Shun</reading> pokes up from his burrow the moment the yard warms, shouts <reading>しゅん</reading>, and dives straight back down out of pure habit. He shuns the cold on principle, but there isn't any today — the mud outside smells exactly like the springtime the person just stepped into.

k-buddhist-temple.meaning_mnemonic: A monk drags a wooden marker across the bare <radical>earth</radical> to claim a plot. He measures it out with a tiny <radical>inch</radical> ruler, one stubborn tick at a time. By sundown the ring of stakes is wide enough for a <kanji>Buddhist temple</kanji>.
k-buddhist-temple.reading_mnemonic: The old groundskeeper everyone calls <reading>Jee</reading>, nobody remembers his real name, is the one who planted the signpost and paced out the whole plot with the inch ruler. Visitors greet him with a friendly <reading>じ</reading> before they even reach the gate. He's older than the temple itself now.

k-head.meaning_mnemonic: A farmer stacks his <radical>beans</radical> on top of a giant <radical>page</radical> torn from his ledger. The stack wobbles and splits into <radical>eight</radical> tumbling piles. One heavy pile crashes down and thumps him square on the <kanji>head</kanji>.
k-head.reading_mnemonic: Back at the desk, a deskmate spots the bump swelling where the log struck. He winces and mutters <reading>とう</reading>, the same hiss you'd make after stubbing your <reading>toe</reading> on a desk leg.

k-valley.meaning_mnemonic: Two mountain slopes lean toward each other and pinch into a single <radical>valley</radical>. Rain runs down both sides and gathers in that low dip. It can never escape, so it fills the whole <kanji>valley</kanji>.
k-valley.reading_mnemonic: At the bottom, the hiker cracks open a can of <reading>coke</reading> and glugs it back with a throaty <reading>こく</reading>, foam sliding down her sleeve while the stone rolls to a stop at her boots.

k-ray.meaning_mnemonic: A shrine held in <radical>esteem</radical> sits on bare <radical>ground</radical>. Two <radical>human legs</radical> climb its steps toward the glow at the top. That glow shoots outward in one long <kanji>ray</kanji> of light.
k-ray.reading_mnemonic: Koichi arrives to restock the shrine's offering box just as the light rays hit his eyes. He shields his face and grunts <reading>こう</reading>, the same rough sound as a crow's <reading>caw</reading> from the shrine roof.

k-round.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>drop</radical> of water lands on a coiled fishing hook shaped like <radical>nine</radical>. The drop pulls the coil tight around itself as it slides in. It curls shut into a perfect <kanji>round</kanji> ball.
k-round.reading_mnemonic: The fisherman reeling in that tight round ball grunts <reading>がん</reading> with every heave, a sound as sharp as a rusty <reading>gun</reading> cocking twice. Neighbors on the riverbank swear they can hear it from their porches.

k-advance.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>old bird</radical> refuses to fly anymore. It hops off its perch onto the winding <radical>road</radical> below. Wings folded, it walks step by step to <kanji>advance</kanji>.
k-advance.reading_mnemonic: Watching the bird finally waddle down the road, an old walker named <reading>Shin</reading> claps once and shouts <reading>しん</reading>, cheering it on like a marathon fan. He falls in behind it, refusing to walk any faster than the bird does.

k-build.meaning_mnemonic: A foreman grips a loaded <radical>brush</radical>, ink dripping from its tip. He drags his back leg into a <radical>long stride or stretching</radical> that no real step should reach. The trailing brush inks one straight line, marking where to <kanji>build</kanji>.
k-build.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting shiba, patrols the fresh foundation line like it is one more sword for his wall. Every lap he barks <reading>けん</reading>, and the crew swears the dog is shouting his own name, <reading>Ken</reading>.

k-cold.meaning_mnemonic: Snow buries the <radical>roof</radical> of the village <radical>well</radical>. A <radical>drop</radical> from the bucket rope freezes solid before it falls. Someone splits firewood into <radical>eight</radical> pieces, but the <kanji>cold</kanji> yard stays frozen anyway.
k-cold.reading_mnemonic: A boy named <reading>Khan</reading> comes to fill his bucket at that same frozen well. His fingers touch the ice and he yelps <reading>かん</reading>, yanking his hand back and blowing on it. His shivering bark echoes off the roof above.

k-copy.meaning_mnemonic: Someone throws a blanket <radical>cover</radical> over the office photocopier's lid. Its glass sits flat as <radical>ground</radical> underneath. The page slides out creased like a stubborn <radical>wrap</radical>, a wrinkled <kanji>copy</kanji>.
k-copy.reading_mnemonic: The office clerk, <reading>Shaw</reading>, peels the crumpled twin off the tray and stares. He hisses one clipped <reading>しゃ</reading> through his teeth, half praise, half warning, and staples it to the original before anyone notices the crease.
k-copy.description: This character covers more than duplicating on paper. It also means being captured or reflected in an image, which is why the same kanji covers photographs and vivid description, not just literal copies.

k-england.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>big</radical> hero stands guard in a patch of <radical>grass</radical>. Rain soaks him, so his only <radical>cover</radical> is a damp blanket knotted like a cape. Freezing and proud, he still calls himself <kanji>England</kanji>.
k-england.reading_mnemonic: A jogger named <reading>Ray</reading> circles the same grassy field and spots the blanket-caped hero still holding his pose in the wind. Ray snorts back a laugh, muttering <reading>えい</reading> under his breath as he jogs on, already composing the story for his friends.
k-england.description: This character originally meant outstanding or brilliant, which is why hero survives as an accepted meaning. Centuries later it was borrowed purely for its sound to write the country name England, a meaning with no real connection to the original character.

k-goods.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> shouts a price for a crate of <radical>goods</radical> in the crowded market. Another mouth shouts back an even higher price. By closing time both have sold every last one of their <kanji>goods</kanji>.
k-goods.reading_mnemonic: An inspector named <reading>Hin</reading> arrives to stamp the stacked crates before they ship. Top crate: a short, sharp <reading>ひん</reading>. Left crate: <reading>ひん</reading>. Right crate: <reading>ひん</reading>. Three stamps, three crates, one approved delivery.
k-goods.description: 品 covers more than merchandise. It can also mean refined bearing or quiet dignity — the sense behind calling someone classy rather than crude. That reading has nothing to do with boxes, so expect 品 to describe character as often as cargo.

k-lower.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> strides forward, then drops into a sudden crouch. They press their <radical>family name</radical> seal onto the <radical>ground</radical> instead of a desk. Bowing that low is what <kanji>lower</kanji> means.
k-lower.reading_mnemonic: Tay, a tortoise whose shell is too heavy to lift, groans <reading>てい</reading> every time he tries to stand. It comes out flat and defeated, like the English word <reading>tay</reading>. He gives up and presses his belly back onto the ground beside the still-bowing person. Down there, low is where he stays.

k-ocean.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Eight</radical> <radical>sheep</radical> stand chewing by the <radical>water</radical>. The water rises and spreads until the fence and the sheep are gone under it. It keeps going, flat and endless, until it is one giant <kanji>ocean</kanji>.
k-ocean.reading_mnemonic: A shepherd named <reading>Yo</reading> wades into the rising water, reaching for his drifting sheep. All he can manage is one long call, <reading>よう</reading>, echoing across the flood.

k-open.meaning_mnemonic: Someone bars the <radical>gate</radical> shut with <radical>two</radical> chopsticks laid flat. A slab of <radical>ground</radical> gets wedged under it by <radical>two hands</radical>, using it like a lever. It tips into a <radical>slide</radical> and the gate flies <kanji>open</kanji>.
k-open.reading_mnemonic: A locksmith named <reading>Kai</reading> turns up once the chopsticks hit the ground. He looks at the busted latch, lets out a low whistle — <reading>かい</reading> — and bolts on a proper lock so it never happens again.

k-people.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>corpse</radical> sprawls on the floor, and the whole party crowd flops down beside it. A clerk stamps every forehead with the same <radical>family name</radical>. They open one tired <radical>mouth</radical> each and groan together as one exhausted crowd of <kanji>people</kanji>.
k-people.reading_mnemonic: One yawning guest, half-asleep, is named <reading>Min</reading>. His yawn trails into a long, drawn-out <reading>みん</reading>. The whole room mumbles it back before collapsing for the night.

k-polish.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>stick</radical> stands in the <radical>ground</radical> like a flagpole. <radical>Two hands</radical> grind it against a <radical>stone</radical> <radical>two</radical> times, and a <radical>barb</radical> flakes off. It slides down a <radical>slide</radical> into an open <radical>mouth</radical>, leaving a bright <kanji>polish</kanji>.
k-polish.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting shiba, drags his favorite blade to the cave and hones it against the newly polished stone. Sparks fly, and he barks out his own name with satisfaction: <reading>Ken</reading>, <reading>けん</reading>.
k-polish.description: In real vocabulary, 研 rarely stands alone as polish. It almost always pairs with another kanji for research or study, carrying over the old sense of grinding at something, a stone or a problem, until it is smooth.

k-possess.meaning_mnemonic: You balance a coin on level <radical>ground</radical>, and it tips into a <radical>slide</radical>. The coin slips down through a window where the <radical>moon</radical> hangs. It drops into your palm, and now you <kanji>possess</kanji> it.
k-possess.reading_mnemonic: On the far side of that same window, a boy named <reading>Yu</reading> catches the falling coin and whoops <reading>ゆう</reading>. He stuffs it straight into his pocket and grins up at the moon, already counting the coin as his.

k-prefecture.meaning_mnemonic: A giant <radical>eye</radical> stares down at one <radical>small</radical> patch of land. It never looks away, guarding only that one stretch of ground. That single watched patch becomes its own <kanji>prefecture</kanji>.
k-prefecture.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting shiba, gets posted to guard that same small patch of land under the staring eye. Every time a stranger's boot crosses the border, he barks <reading>けん</reading>, sharp as the English name <reading>Ken</reading> shouted twice. He never abandons his post. The eye above never blinks either.

k-products.meaning_mnemonic: Under a <radical>cliff</radical>, a peddler takes her <radical>stand</radical> guarding a pot with a <radical>lid</radical>. A shoot of <radical>life</radical> pushes up and splits it into <radical>eight</radical> pieces. By morning her stall overflows with <kanji>products</kanji>.
k-products.reading_mnemonic: A customer at the stall picks up the split log and says it looks freshly <reading>sawn</reading>, <reading>さん</reading>, right down the middle. She buys every product on the counter before the sawdust even settles.

k-public-chamber.meaning_mnemonic: The plaza of <radical>earth</radical> is held in high <radical>esteem</radical> by the whole town. A crowd fills it, too big for the open sky above. Someone stretches a giant <radical>cover</radical> across it, and it becomes the <kanji>public chamber</kanji>.
k-public-chamber.reading_mnemonic: Under the same blanket-roofed hall, a baker elbows in holding a fresh lump of <reading>dough</reading>, insisting the shrine crowd taste it. Everyone groans one long <reading>どう</reading>, half hunger, half surrender, and makes room for him anyway.
k-public-chamber.description: This kanji almost never stands alone. In real use it is nearly always the second half of a compound naming one specific large room — a dining hall, a lecture hall — rather than a generic public chamber on its own.

k-research.meaning_mnemonic: You climb into a dark <radical>cave</radical> holding a hook bent like <radical>nine</radical>. You lower the hook and search along the floor for the bottom. Digging that deep for answers is called <kanji>research</kanji>.
k-research.reading_mnemonic: Word gets out about the cave, and a <reading>queue</reading> forms at its mouth — everyone wants a turn with the hook. Each hopeful calls out <reading>きゅう</reading> to mark their place in line, over and over, until it's finally your turn.
k-research.description: The kun reading きわ also appears in an unrelated verb with the same pronunciation, meaning to pursue something to its absolute limit. Context is what tells the two apart, not sound.

k-ride.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>stick</radical> planted in the <radical>ground</radical> holds up a heavy bundle of <radical>grain</radical>. Suddenly it snaps into <radical>eight</radical> pieces. You leap onto the falling grain and <kanji>ride</kanji> it down the hill like a sled.
k-ride.reading_mnemonic: At the bottom of the hill, the sled skids to a stop. A conductor named <reading>Jo</reading> is waiting. He blows his whistle and drags out one long boarding call: <reading>じょう</reading>. You climb aboard for another ride.

k-rouse.meaning_mnemonic: You lean against a gate stuck at a dead <radical>stop</radical>. A whistle cracks at dawn, and your legs launch straight into a <radical>run</radical>. You leap the gate and <kanji>rouse</kanji> yourself awake.
k-rouse.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit lives in the trunk beside that same gate. Your sudden sprint sends leaves raining down. She pokes her head out and calls <reading>き</reading> after you, giggling her own name, <reading>Kiki</reading>. She's delighted someone finally got up and running before dawn.

k-short.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>arrow</radical> hits a target and snaps in half, the pieces splitting apart like <radical>eight</radical>. The stub falls into a bowl of <radical>beans</radical> and looks tiny beside a whole one. Cut off before its time, the little arrow stays <kanji>short</kanji>.
k-short.reading_mnemonic: The vendor is a wiry guy everyone calls <reading>Tan</reading>. Every time he pulls another snapped stub from the bowl, he mutters <reading>たん</reading> under his breath. He's annoyed at how short his profits look today.
k-short.description: Beyond literal shortness, 短 also carries the sense of a shortcoming. It's the kind of short that comes up when someone lists a personality flaw or weak point, not just a measurement of length.

k-silver.meaning_mnemonic: Workers stack bars of <radical>gold</radical> in the vault. The inspector's boot hits an immovable <radical>stopping</radical> point at one duller bar. She sets that reject aside and calls it <kanji>silver</kanji>.
k-silver.reading_mnemonic: The vault inspector introduces herself as <reading>Gin</reading>. She says it the same flat way every time she rejects a bar, <reading>ぎん</reading>, like she's already bored of the job. She's the one who decided, years ago, that silver deserved its own shelf.

k-sino.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>big</radical> man kneels on the <radical>ground</radical> beside a river of <radical>water</radical>. He plants <radical>two</radical> stalks of <radical>grass</radical> in it and opens his <radical>mouth</radical> to sing. His song names this whole land <kanji>China</kanji>.
k-sino.reading_mnemonic: By the river, the scholar seals his finished scroll inside a battered tin <reading>can</reading> to keep out the damp. He raps the lid twice and it rings out <reading>かん</reading>, <reading>かん</reading>, echoing over the water. That hollow knock is the sound stamped on every character he writes.
k-sino.description: 漢 rarely stands by itself. It usually works as a bound prefix meaning Chinese or Sino-, attached ahead of another kanji rather than standing alone. In some older compounds the same character can also simply mean "a man" or "fellow," with no connection to China at all.

k-substitute.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> dreads standing guard all night at the <radical>ceremony</radical>. They stuff a coat with straw and lean it against the post instead. Nobody notices the swap, and the dummy becomes their <kanji>substitute</kanji>.
k-substitute.reading_mnemonic: Dai, the giant baby, truck-sized, toddles up and spots the straw double leaned against the post. He points and wails <reading>だい</reading>, landing like the English word <reading>dye</reading> spilled across the square. The ground trembles with every sob. The straw substitute never even flinches.

k-sultry.meaning_mnemonic: Through the window you watch the <radical>sun</radical> blaze over the crosswalk. An <radical>old</radical> man shuffles across without hurrying for anyone. The asphalt shimmers in the thick <kanji>sultry</kanji> air.
k-sultry.reading_mnemonic: The kid waiting beside him is named <reading>Sho</reading>. He wilts in the heat and groans <reading>しょ</reading> under his breath. He wishes the old man would hurry so the signal would finally let him escape the sun.
k-sultry.description: This kanji is only used for the sultry heat of weather or air: a stifling afternoon, a muggy room. It never describes a hot object, a hot drink, or a fever. Those use a different word entirely.

k-vegetable.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>claw</radical> reaches down through <radical>grass</radical> under a <radical>tree</radical>. It rips up whatever roots it finds there. Whatever the claw pulls free becomes tonight's <kanji>vegetable</kanji>.
k-vegetable.reading_mnemonic: The taste-tester, <reading>Sai</reading>, forks up the tree-claw's tangled grass dish and chews. His face falls. He exhales one long <reading>さい</reading>, not hunger, just regret, and quietly pushes the rest to the dog.

k-ward.meaning_mnemonic: Ink shoots down a <radical>slide</radical> and falls as one round <radical>drop</radical>. It splashes into a <radical>box on its side</radical> and fills it edge to edge. The ink stays penned inside, marking off its own <kanji>ward</kanji>.
k-ward.reading_mnemonic: A pigeon named Coo waddles to the top of the slide and loses her footing. She drops straight down, cooing <reading>く</reading> the whole way, soft as an English <reading>coo</reading>. She lands smack inside the tipped-over box, wings pinned flat to its walls. Coo is boxed into her own little ward now.
